title: First aid essentials
summary: Quick steps for checking a casualty, adult CPR and AED use, choking, severe bleeding with a tourniquet, burns, electric shock, heat stroke, hypothermia and suspected spine injury. It always starts with calling for help if it can be reached, and it is no substitute for a certified first aid course.

steps.text: Make the scene safe, call 9-1-1 first if help can be reached, then check response, airway and breathing.
steps.warn: Do not step into live wires, fire, gas or traffic. If you are hurt you cannot help.

steps.text: Find the problem in the headings: CPR, choking, bleeding, shock, burns, electric shock, heat or cold, spine.
Keep checking breathing and responsiveness until help takes over. Write down times, such as when a tourniquet went on.
Check your kit every 90 days and take a certified first aid course; reading is not training.

notes:
## Call first

**If help can be reached, call it first.** In Canada and the US that is 9-1-1. Use speaker and follow the dispatcher (HSF). Call for anyone unresponsive, not breathing normally, bleeding badly, or with chest pain, a seizure, or a head, neck, back or pelvis injury (CRC). If no help is coming, see [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_first_aid/when_no_help_is_coming). This card does not replace a first aid course.

## Check the casualty

1. **Danger.** Is the scene safe for you? Use gloves or a barrier if you have them (CRC).
2. **Response.** Tap the shoulders and shout "Are you OK?" (AHA).
3. **Airway.** No response: tilt the head back and lift the chin (CRC).
4. **Breathing.** Watch the chest for 5 to 10 s. Gasping is not normal breathing: treat it as no breathing (CRC, AHA).
5. **Bleeding.** Scan head to toe for life-threatening bleeding (CRC).

## Adult CPR and AED

Start if unresponsive and not breathing normally.

| Item | What to do |
|---|---|
| Alone | Call 9-1-1 and fetch the AED yourself (CRC) |
| Hands | Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top (CRC) |
| Rate | 100 to 120 per minute; 30 pushes take about 15 to 18 s (AHA, CRC) |
| Depth | At least 5 cm (2 in). Let the chest rise fully each time (AHA, CRC) |
| Ratio | 30 compressions, then 2 breaths (AHA, CRC) |
| Breaths | Open airway, barrier over mouth, just enough air to make the chest start to rise. If they will not go in, do 30 pushes, look in the mouth, remove any object you see (CRC) |
| Pauses | Never more than 10 s (AHA) |
| No breaths | If unwilling or unable, compressions only, non-stop (CRC, HSF) |
| AED | Turn on, follow the prompts. Dry a wet chest. Pads at least 2.5 cm (1 in) from a pacemaker. Nobody touching during a shock. Then restart compressions (CRC) |
| Stop when | EMS or someone else takes over, you are too tired, the scene turns unsafe, or the person clearly moves (CRC) |

**Recovery position:** breathing but unresponsive? Roll them onto their side as one unit, support the head, recheck breathing (CRC).

## Choking (adult)

Can cough or speak: encourage coughing (CRC). Cannot speak, cough or breathe:

1. Call 9-1-1 as soon as someone can.
2. Alternate up to 5 back blows (lean them forward, firm blows between the shoulder blades) with up to 5 abdominal thrusts (fist just above the navel, quick inward and upward). Chest thrusts are an accepted alternative (CRC).
3. Unresponsive: start CPR with compressions (CRC).
4. Alone: call, then thrust your own abdomen against a firm object (CRC).

## Severe bleeding

1. Call 9-1-1. Expose the wound.
2. Press hard on a clean cloth or dressing with both hands until responders take over. If it soaks through, add more on top (ACS, CRC).
3. Deep wound, or neck, shoulder or groin: pack with gauze (clotting gauze preferred) or clean cloth, then press with both hands (ACS).
4. **Tourniquet** (arm or leg only) if pressure fails, you cannot reach the wound, or you must move the person (CRC):
   - Place 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) above the wound, never on a joint (ACS, CRC). If unsure, as high on the limb as possible (Ready.gov).
   - Tighten until bleeding stops. It will hurt (ACS, CRC).
   - **Write down the time** (ACS, CRC).
   - Still bleeding: add a second one. Leave them on until EMS takes over (Ready.gov).

## Shock

Signs: confusion, cool clammy skin, weakness, fast breathing, thirst, drowsiness (CRC). Call 9-1-1, treat the cause, keep warm, loosen tight clothing. If conscious with no head, neck, spine or leg injury, lay flat and raise the legs about 30 cm (12 in). No food or drink (MedlinePlus).

## Burns

- Cool with cool (not freezing) water or a clean cool compress for **at least 10 minutes** (CRC, CCOHS).
- Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn, not anything stuck. Cover loosely with a dry sterile dressing (CRC).
- **Never** use ice, butter, creams or sprays. Do not break blisters (MassDPH).
- Call 9-1-1 for burns that affect breathing, are chemical, explosive or electrical, are deep or very blistered, or cover the face, neck, hands, genitals or a large area (CRC).
- Chemical: remove contaminated clothing, brush off dry powder, flush with cool running water for **at least 15 minutes** (CRC).

## Electric shock

1. **Look first, do not touch.** Current can pass to you (CDC).
2. Switch off at the breaker or fuse box. Switching off the appliance is not enough (CCOHS).
3. If you cannot, push the source away with dry wood, cardboard or plastic (CDC).
4. Call 9-1-1. Check breathing. CPR if it has stopped (CDC).
5. Look for entry and exit burns and cover them. Keep the person still (CRC, CCOHS).
6. Never touch a fallen power line. Stay at least 10 m (33 ft) from it and from anyone touching it, and call the utility (CDC, NB Power).

## Heat and cold

| Problem | Signs | Do |
|---|---|---|
| Heat stroke | Hot skin (dry or damp), 39.4 °C (103 °F) or more, confusion, fainting, seizures (CDC, CRC) | Call 9-1-1. Shade, remove outer clothes, cool fast: cold wet cloths, ice packs on armpits and chest, fan. Keep cooling until help comes. Nothing to drink (CDC) |
| Hypothermia | Shivering, fumbling, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness. Below 35 °C (95 °F) is an emergency (CDC) | Handle gently, keep flat, remove wet clothes, insulate, warm the chest, neck and head. Don’t rub the arms and legs or put them in a hot bath. No alcohol. Food or drink only if fully alert. Check breathing for up to 60 s in severe cases; not breathing: CPR, keep warming (CDC, CRC) |

## Suspected spine injury

Suspect it after a fall from more than the person's height, a dive, a hard blow to the head, jaw or torso, lightning or electric shock (CRC). Call 9-1-1. Keep them still, support the head as found, and move them only if you must (CRC, CCOHS). If they vomit, log-roll with head, neck and back in line (MedlinePlus). Life threats such as no breathing come first (CRC).

## Basic kit

- Non-latex gloves, CPR face shield or pocket mask (CRC, WorkSafeNB)
- Gauze pads, pressure dressings, roller and triangular bandages with pins, tape, plasters (WorkSafeNB, CRC)
- Scissors, tweezers, antiseptic wipes, emergency blanket, flashlight (CRC)
- Tourniquet and clotting gauze for a trauma kit (ACS)

Check it every 90 days and after use. Replace expired items (WorkSafeNB).

## When no help is coming

**Beyond first aid** below means you can only buy time: protect the person from cold, keep them still, give drinks only if they are fully alert and not vomiting, and take them to the most skilled person you can reach. For heat stroke, cool them first.

### Decide: stay or go

Go early, not once they fail. Go for breathing trouble, shock, falling alertness, any broken bone or a limb that loses circulation, movement or feeling, suspected spine injury, a head blow with any blackout, a fall over 4.5 m (15 ft), spreading infection, vomiting or diarrhoea over 12 hours (start rehydration at once, see Dehydration and diarrhoea), fever over 38.9 °C (102 °F), or burns to face, hands, feet or genitals. Carries are slow and dangerous. A simple one- or two-person carry is not acceptable with a neck injury (NOLS-Evac).

**Write it down:** time of each check, alertness, breathing, pulse, skin, pupils, each change and what you did. Hand it to the next carer (NOLS-SOAP).

### CPR when no help is coming

| Case | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Do not start | Danger to you. Injuries no one survives (head severed, body cut in two, whole body burned, decomposed, frozen solid). Stiff body or blood pooled low, unless very cold (MRA, ICAR, NAEMSP, WMS-Hypo). If in doubt, start (ICRC-FA) |
| Stop | Someone takes over, you are exhausted or in danger, or no response after about 30 min (MRA). Not for a person who may be hypothermic: do not stop at 30 min, keep going as long as you safely can (WMS-Hypo). At 20 min if the collapse was unwitnessed, no AED shock was advised and they are not cold (ICAR) |
| Major injury | A heart that stops after a major wound is usually from blood loss, so CPR rarely helps (ICRC-FA). If death is not obvious, stop visible bleeding first, then give CPR (ICRC-FA). Do not apply this to drowning, lightning, cold, or a collapse that may not be from the injury: treat those as any cardiac arrest (NAEMSP). Stopping is allowed with no sign of life and no response to CPR (NAEMSP) |
| Drowning | Give breaths too. Stopping may be reasonable after 25 min of continuous CPR, depending on the situation, but not for someone who may be hypothermic (WMS-Drown, WMS-Hypo) |

### Bleeding over hours

- A tourniquet carries little risk for about 2 hours. Most limbs tolerate up to about 6, but the risk of lasting damage rises after 3 to 4 hours. Never loosen it now and then (WMS-Wound, TCCC).
- **Converting** it to a pressure dressing is for a trained responder: within 2 hours, and only if the person is not in shock, the wound can be watched, and it is not an amputation. Dress first, ease it off, leave it loose 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) above. If bleeding returns, tighten it and stop. After 6 hours, do not remove it outside a closely monitored setting (TCCC, WMS-Wound).
- Not trained, or unsure: **leave it on**, write the time, go to skilled care (WMS-Wound, TCCC).

### Wounds

- Irrigate early with clean drinking water, at least 1 L (34 fl oz), as a forceful syringe jet if possible. Add nothing (WMS-Wound). WHO disaster guidance washes for 10 min with soap and boiled water, then rinses (WHO-Wound).
- **Leave open and cover** a wound that is soil-contaminated, a bite, over 6 hours old, or has pus. Pack loosely with damp clean gauze under a dry dressing. Change it at least daily (WHO-Wound, WMS-Wound). Only a clean wound under 6 hours old may be closed, which is beyond first aid (WMS-Wound).
- Infection: more redness, swelling, pain, discharge or pus (CRC, NOLS-Evac, WHO-Wound). Spreading: red streaks toward the heart, swollen glands, fever, confusion, crackling under the skin (NOLS-Evac, WMS-Wound). **Beyond first aid.**

### Burns over days

- Cool with clean, cool (not cold) water for up to 20 min. No ice (WMS-Burns).
- Leave blisters whole. Cover with a clean, dry, non-stick dressing, between burned fingers and toes too. Never wrap tight round a limb (WMS-Burns, ICRC-FA).
- If help is far, change it about every 2 days. If it sticks, soak it with clean water first (ICRC-FA).
- Keep warm. Drink plenty if alert and not vomiting; over about 20 % of the body, sip oral rehydration solution (WMS-Burns, ICRC-FA).
- **Beyond first aid:** infection (fever, spreading redness, pus), or a burn over about 10 % of the body (their palm is 1 %), on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, deep, electrical, chemical, smoke, or all round a limb (WMS-Burns, WMS-Wound, NOLS-Evac).

### Fractures and dislocations

- Splint a break or dislocation in the position found, padded, past the joints above and below. Check colour and warmth below before and after; loosen if cold (CRC).
- Bone through the skin, thigh bone or pelvis: **beyond first aid** (WMS-Wound, CRC).

### Suspected spine injury

WMS sees no role for rigid collars and uses a backboard only to move someone briefly, not to hold them still: limit movement, do not lock the person in place. Trained people use NEXUS or the Canadian C-spine rule (WMS-Spine). **Protect the neck if any is true** (NEXUS): midline neck tenderness, weakness, numbness or tingling, not fully alert, drunk or drugged, another painful injury. After blunt injury, none means low risk, not cleared (NEXUS, WMS-Spine). Keep head and neck in line, never forced; side-lying if the airway is at risk, such as vomiting (WMS-Spine).

### Cold and heat

**Hypothermia** (WMS-Hypo)

- Handle gently, keep flat. No early standing or walking.
- Insulate under and around, add a plastic or tarp barrier, cover head and neck, cut off wet clothes once sheltered.
- Heat to the trunk: large warm pads or water bottles at chest, armpits and back, cloth between. Check skin every 20 to 30 min. Not arms and legs. No hot bath or shower.
- Alert and shivering: warm sweet food and drink, rest about 30 min.
- Unresponsive: check breathing and pulse for a full minute before CPR. Stiffness and fixed pupils do not prove death in the cold. Moving them: CPR in blocks of 5 min or more, pauses no longer than 5 min.

**Heat stroke:** whole-body cold-water immersion cools fastest. Use ice water or the coldest you can find (WMS-Heat, AAFP). No tub: strip, soak the skin in cold water and fan hard; this is about half as fast. Never delay cooling for drinks. Stop at a core temperature of about 38.3 to 38.8 °C (WMS-Heat). With no thermometer, cool until thinking clears: 15 minutes is a guide, not a limit (ILCOR).

### Dehydration and diarrhoea

**WHO home recipe:** 1 L (34 fl oz) clean drinking water, 6 teaspoons sugar, ½ teaspoon salt (WHO-ORS, WHO-Cholera). Plain water alone is not enough, but with no sugar or salt the most important thing is to keep the person drinking safe fluids (WHO-Cholera). Measure with care: serious errors can happen with homemade mixes, so use ORS packets if you have them (CDC-ORS). Keep sipping after vomiting, and keep eating (WHO-Cholera, WHO-Diarrhoea). Urgent: very sleepy, cannot drink, confused. **Beyond first aid:** severe dehydration needs a drip. Blood in the stool, or diarrhoea over 14 days, needs skilled care (WHO-Diarrhoea, WHO-Cholera).

### When someone dies

- **Be sure.** Keep helping until a health professional confirms death, or all of these are true: no breathing, no pulse, wide pupils that ignore light, no movement, a cold body (ICRC-FA). None of these signs can be trusted in a person who is very cold or was in cold water: they can look dead and not be, so keep going (WMS-Hypo).
- Note time and place. Cover the body and follow their customs (ICRC-FA).
- Bodies of people killed by injury, drowning or fire do not start epidemics, but can foul drinking water. Someone who died of an infectious disease such as cholera can still infect: handle the body as little as possible, keep relatives from touching it, and wear eye protection, gloves and boots (ICRC-Dead, WHO-TN8). Otherwise wear gloves if you have them. Wash hands with soap and clean water (ICRC-Dead).
- With no authority, bury about 1.5 m (5 ft) deep, at least 200 m (650 ft) from drinking water. Mark and record the grave (ICRC-Dead).
